title: TRUE and FALSE: what a comparison returns

screens.prompt: In B9, answer TRUE when the total units are over 100.

hints.syntax: =SUM(B2:B7)>100 — the comparison wraps the total, not the other way round.
hints.func-sum: The question is about the total, so the units have to be added up inside the formula.
hints.require-ref: Add the units column in the grid rather than typing the total.
hints.value: The six items add to 150, which is over 100, so the answer is TRUE.
hints.error: Dividing by zero anywhere in the comparison returns #DIV/0!.

reject.why: the words TRUE and FALSE are text, not the logical values
the comparison points the wrong way, so it answers FALSE
typing the answer as text never adds anything up
the range starts on row 3, so the first item is left out of the total
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the range sits outside the parentheses

screens.prompt: In B9, answer TRUE when the average units are at least 20.

hints.syntax: =AVERAGE(B2:B7)>=20 — the comparison wraps the whole calculation.
hints.func-average: The question is about the average, so a total cannot answer it.
hints.require-ref: Take the average over the units column of the grid.
hints.value: The six items average 25 units, which is at least 20, so the answer is TRUE.
hints.error: A division by zero in the range returns #DIV/0! instead of a logical value.

reject.why: the total is 150 and would pass almost any threshold, which is not the question
the average is 25, so a stricter threshold answers FALSE
the range starts on row 3, so the first item is left out of the average
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the words TRUE and FALSE are text, not the logical values
the range sits outside the parentheses

docs.syntax: =SUM(B2:B7)>100 returns TRUE or FALSE; it is the comparison, not a word
docs.explain: Every comparison in Excel is itself a formula, and it hands back one of two logical values rather than the words TRUE and FALSE. Type =SUM(B2:B7)>100 and the cell holds TRUE, formatted in capitals, and the same value can be used by IF, by AND, or by a conditional format without ever being written as text. Because the logical values are not text, a formula that returns the string "TRUE" looks right and behaves differently: it will not drive IF, it will not count as a match for TRUE, and sorting puts it in with the words. In this drill the units add to 150, so =SUM(B2:B7)>100 answers TRUE, while the second screen wraps an average in the same comparison and answers TRUE because the six items average 25 units. Both screens are drills in reading the question: the comparison operator carries the whole meaning, and putting an IF around it only wraps a value that was already Boolean. The common failure is writing the words in quotes, which is the one form that grades as a wrong answer here.

errors.text: Text and a number were compared with an operator that cannot order them.
The comparison divided by zero before it produced a value.

docs.atWork: Flagging a month as over budget without adding a helper column of yes and no words.
docs.outcome: Read a comparison as a TRUE or FALSE value you can build on, not as text.
docs.teaches: comparison operators returning logical values, and why quoted TRUE is not one
